periods.activity_title: Tiling the Room: Rediscovering Factors and Common Factors

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: section 11.1 p.48
textbook_items_in_class.description: 'Jump Jackpot' game: for treasures on (a) 14 and 30; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 30 and 50; (d) 28 and 42, find the longest jump size from 0 that lands on both numbers, and explain why it equals their HCF.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 11.1 p.52
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the common factors and HCF of 45 and 75. Using 45 = 3×3×5 and 75 = 3×5×5, the common subparts are 3, 5, 15, so common factors are 1, 3, 5, 15 and HCF = 15.

time_bands.activity: Pose the room-tiling situation: a 12 ft × 16 ft floor must be covered by the largest possible whole-number square tile. Students list whole-number common factors of 12 and 16 by inspection, then identify the greatest. The concrete scenario anchors the abstract definition of the Highest Common Factor as the greatest of the common factors of two numbers.

section 11.1 p.48 ("'Jump Jackpot' game: for treasures on (a) 14 and 30....") — pairs play parts (a) and (b) on a number line drawn in their books, writing which jump sizes land on both numbers and circling the longest. Class compares results, naming the pattern observed.

Walk through Example 1, section 11.1 p.52 ("Find the common factors and HCF of 45 and 75...."). Students follow the prime-factorisation steps for 45 and 75, identify the common prime subparts (single 3 and single 5, giving 3, 5, 15), and confirm HCF = 15. They re-express the rule: the HCF is built from each prime shared by both numbers, taken as few times as it appears in either.

Students attempt Jump Jackpot parts (c) and (d) from section 11.1 p.48 ("'Jump Jackpot' game....") independently, writing the prime factorisations of each pair before identifying the common factors. Brief whole-class check of answers.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who confuse factors of a number with multiples; the tiling story helps because a tile side must divide the room dimension exactly. A common error at this stage is listing 6 as a common factor of 12 and 16 — a quick check by division corrects it. For a self-study follow-up, Example 2, section 11.1 p.52 gives a parallel worked case with different prime structures.

periods.activity_title: Prime Factorisation as a Tool: Building the Factor Tree

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 11.1 p.51
textbook_items_in_class.description: List all the factors of (a) 90; (b) 105; (c) 132; (d) 360 (24 factors); (e) 840 (32 factors), using prime factorisation.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 2, section 11.1 p.52
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the common factors and HCF of 112 and 84. Using 112 = 2×2×2×2×7 and 84 = 2×2×3×7, the largest common subpart is 2×2×7 = 28, so HCF = 28.

time_bands.activity: Recall that Anshu conjectured larger numbers always have longer prime factorisations. Students predict whether 121 has more prime factors than 90, then compute: 121 = 11×11 and 90 = 2×3×3×5, yielding three distinct primes for 90 versus one for 121. The counterexample shows the conjecture is false and motivates careful prime factorisation.

Figure it Out, section 11.1 p.51 ("List all the factors of (a) 90; (b) 105; (c) 132....") — students work on parts (a) and (b) in pairs, using the compact division method to find primes first, then systematically listing all factor combinations. Each pair checks that the count of factors matches expectations.

Walk through Example 2, section 11.1 p.52 ("Find the common factors and HCF of 112 and 84...."). On the board, align 112 = 2⁴×7 and 84 = 2²×3×7 vertically; students identify the largest common subpart 2²×7 = 28 and verify 112 ÷ 28 = 4 and 84 ÷ 28 = 3.

Students attempt Figure it Out, section 11.1 p.51 ("List all the factors of....") part (c) on 132 individually, writing the prime factorisation first and then building the factor list. Teacher circulates, checking whether factors are systematically enumerated or haphazardly listed.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often stop factorising too early, writing 4×3×11 for 132 instead of continuing to 2×2×3×11. Emphasise that every factor in the expression must be a prime. The 840 = 2³×3×5×7 case in Figure it Out part (e) is an excellent challenge for confident students to attempt as self-study.

periods.activity_title: Computing HCF by Prime Factorisation: Practice and Pitfalls

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 11.1 p.53
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the common factors and HCF of (a) 50, 60; (b) 140, 275; (c) 77, 725; (d) 370, 592; (e) 81, 243.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 11.1 p.54
Example 3, section 11.1 p.53
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the common factors and HCF of 96 and 275. Since 96 = 2×2×2×2×2×3 and 275 = 5×5×11 share no prime subpart, the only common factor is 1, which is also the HCF.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 11.1 p.54
homework.description: Given 72 = 6×12 and 144 = 8×18, decide whether one can conclude the two numbers have no common factor other than 1, and explain why not.

time_bands.activity: Walk through Example 3, section 11.1 p.53 ("Find the common factors and HCF of 96 and 275...."). Students see that sharing no prime factor means HCF = 1, introducing co-prime pairs as a named concept.

Figure it Out, section 11.1 p.53 ("Find the common factors and HCF of (a) 50, 60; (b) 140, 275....") — students work parts (a)–(c) individually, writing prime factorisations before identifying common primes. Pairs swap and verify each other's HCF.

Figure it Out Q1, section 11.1 p.54 ("Find the HCF of (a) 24, 180; (b) 42, 75, 24....") — teacher models part (b) involving three numbers on the board, showing that the rule extends naturally: take each prime the minimum number of times it appears across all three factorisations. Students then complete parts (a) and (c).

Class discusses Figure it Out, section 11.1 p.53 part (d) on 370 and 592, which has a less obvious prime structure. Pairs share their factorisation routes; teacher highlights how the division method handles larger numbers more efficiently than factor trees.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is taking the maximum rather than the minimum exponent when assembling the HCF from prime factorisations — reinforce the contrast with LCM early. Example 4, section 11.1 p.53 and Example 5, section 11.1 p.53 are compact worked cases students can consult independently for additional models of the minimum-exponent rule.

periods.activity_title: Shortest Common Length: Discovering the LCM

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: section 11.2 p.56
textbook_items_in_class.description: 'Idli-Vada' game: for the number pairs (a) 4 and 6; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 14 and 30; (d) 15 and 55, find the first number for which 'idli-vada' is called out, and decide whether the answer is always the LCM.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 6, section 11.2 p.56–57
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the LCM of 14 and 35. From 14 = 2×7 and 35 = 5×7, the LCM must contain 2×7 and 5×7 as subparts: the lowest is 2×5×7 = 70.

time_bands.activity: Present the toran story: Anshu and Guna cut cloth strips of 6 cm and 8 cm to make garlands of equal length. Students list the first several multiples of 6 and 8 in two columns, circle the common ones, and identify the smallest — 24 cm. This introduces the Lowest Common Multiple as the least among all common multiples of two numbers.

section 11.2 p.56 ("'Idli-Vada' game: for the number pairs (a) 4 and 6; (b) 7 and 11....") — students call out counts in pairs, one tagging multiples of the first number and the other tagging multiples of the second, recording the first joint tag. They then verify whether the result equals the LCM in each case and discuss why listing multiples becomes impractical for larger numbers.

Walk through Example 6, section 11.2 p.56–57 ("Find the LCM of 14 and 35...."). Students write 14 = 2×7 and 35 = 5×7 side by side, reason that a common multiple must contain both as subparts, and see that 2×5×7 = 70 is the smallest such product. The key principle — take each prime the maximum number of times it appears in either factorisation — is stated explicitly.

Students revisit the sweet-shop gajak problem embedded in the section (free every 7 days, visited every 10 days) and write the LCM of 7 and 10 using prime factorisations, confirming the answer is 70 days. Teacher asks whether a common multiple less than 70 is possible, and students justify why not.

periods.teacher_notes: Students routinely confuse the Idli-Vada result with the product of the two numbers; emphasise that the LCM is less than or equal to the product and equals it only when the two numbers share no prime factor. Having established the HCF rule as a minimum-exponent procedure, the maximum-exponent contrast for LCM is the key conceptual pivot here.

periods.activity_title: Computing LCM for Pairs and Triples

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 11.2 p.58
Example 7, section 11.2 p.57
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the LCM of 96 and 360. From 96 = 2×2×2×2×2×3 and 360 = 2×2×2×3×3×5, take the maximum occurrences of each prime (five 2s, two 3s, one 5): LCM = 1440.

time_bands.activity: Walk through Example 7, section 11.2 p.57 ("Find the LCM of 96 and 360...."). Teacher writes both factorisations in aligned rows, underlines the maximum occurrences of each prime, and assembles LCM = 2⁵×3²×5 = 1440. Students verify: 1440 ÷ 96 = 15 and 1440 ÷ 360 = 4, confirming it is a multiple of both.

Figure it Out, section 11.2 p.58 ("Find the LCM of (a) 30, 72; (b) 36, 54....") — students work parts (a) and (b) independently, writing full prime factorisations before selecting maximum exponents. Pairs compare and resolve any disagreement before the teacher confirms.

Students tackle Figure it Out, section 11.2 p.58 part (c) on three numbers (105, 195, 65), extending the maximum-exponent rule to a third factorisation. Teacher circulates, prompting students to write all three factorisations in a table before identifying the maximum power of each prime.

Quick whole-class check of Figure it Out, section 11.2 p.58 part (d) on 222 and 370. Students present their prime factorisations and the resulting LCM, with peers confirming by dividing the LCM by each original number.

periods.teacher_notes: Extending to three numbers in part (c) is the key stretch: students sometimes take the maximum prime from only two of the three numbers, omitting the third. Encourage writing all three factorisations in aligned columns so no prime row is skipped. Example 6, section 11.2 p.56–57 is available as a self-study model for students who need to consolidate the two-number case before attempting three.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: Making General Statements: When is the HCF the Smaller Number?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.59
textbook_items_in_class.description: Make and explain a general statement about the HCF of (a) two consecutive even numbers; (b) two consecutive odd numbers; (c) two even numbers; (d) two consecutive numbers; (e) two co-prime numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 11.3 p.59
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given that the LCM of 3 and 24 is 24: (a) find more pairs where the LCM is one of the two numbers; (b) make a general statement about such numbers and describe them using algebra.

time_bands.activity: Pose the opening observation of section 11.3: when one number is a factor of the other — say 6 and 30 — the HCF is the smaller. Students test three more such pairs, then write a general statement in their own words. Teacher formalises using algebra: if one number is n and the other is 5n, the HCF = n.

Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.59 ("Make and explain a general statement about the HCF of (a) two consecutive even numbers....") — students work in groups of three, each group taking two parts. After testing at least four specific numerical cases per part, each group writes a general statement and identifies whether a counterexample is possible.

Figure it Out Q2, section 11.3 p.59 ("Given that the LCM of 3 and 24 is 24....") — students find more pairs where the LCM equals one member, then write the algebraic description (n and kn have LCM = kn). Teacher connects this to the earlier HCF pattern: when one is a multiple of the other, both the HCF and LCM have exact descriptions.

Each group shares its general statement from Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.59. Class evaluates each statement by testing it on a new numerical case not used in drafting. Where a statement fails the new test, the group revises it collaboratively.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often treat a pattern observed in two or three examples as automatically general — this is the key reasoning habit to build here. Prompt with 'Can you find any pair of consecutive odd numbers whose HCF is not 1?' to push towards genuine justification rather than conjecture. The vocabulary 'generalisation' and 'general statement' are introduced in the section text and should be used consistently.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: What Happens When Both Numbers are Doubled? Reasoning About the HCF

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 11.3 p.59
textbook_items_in_class.description: Make and explain a general statement about the LCM of (a) two multiples of 3; (b) two consecutive even numbers; (c) two consecutive numbers; (d) two co-prime numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: section 11.3 p.62
textbook_items_in_class.description: For (a) 45, 105; (b) 275, 352; (c) 222, 370, explore whether the LCM is a factor of the product, find the multiplier that gives the product, and observe that it is the HCF (suggesting HCF × LCM = product).

time_bands.activity: Students take a specific pair — say 6 and 10 with HCF = 2 — and double both to get 12 and 20 with HCF = 4. They repeat with two more pairs of their choice. From these cases they form a conjecture: doubling both numbers doubles the HCF. Teacher asks them to justify this using prime factorisations, showing that a factor of 2 enters every prime power.

Figure it Out Q3, section 11.3 p.59 ("Make and explain a general statement about the LCM of (a) two multiples of 3....") — students work parts (a)–(c) in pairs, testing concrete cases and attempting to state the pattern algebraically. Teacher focuses class attention on part (d) — co-prime numbers — as the anchor case connecting to LCM = product.

section 11.3 p.62 ("For (a) 45, 105; (b) 275, 352; (c) 222, 370, explore whether the LCM is a factor of the product....") — students compute HCF × LCM and the product of the two numbers for each pair, recording results in a table. The pattern HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers emerges from their own calculations.

Teacher leads a brief explanation of why HCF × LCM = product, using the prime-factorisation view: common primes go to the HCF (minimum times), non-common go to the LCM (maximum times), and together they account for all prime factors in both numbers exactly once each. Students write the key property in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes check the property only for co-prime pairs where HCF = 1 and LCM = product, making it seem trivial — steer towards pairs with a non-trivial HCF such as 45 and 105. The question of whether HCF × LCM = product extends to three numbers (posed in the section) is a rich extension for confident students.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: The Combined Division Procedure: An Efficient Route to HCF and LCM

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.63
textbook_items_in_class.description: In two rows of repeating coloured stars, determine when the blue stars will next meet.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 11.3 p.63
Figure it Out Q3, section 11.3 p.63
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the HCF and LCM (stating answers as prime factorisations) of (a) 3×3×5×7×7 and 12×7×11; (b) 45 and 36.

time_bands.activity: Demonstrate the combined division procedure from section 11.3: write both numbers side by side and divide by common primes simultaneously until the quotients share no common factor. Read the HCF from the divisors and the LCM from the divisors combined with the final quotients. Show Guna's shortcut of dividing by a composite common factor (e.g., 50 at once rather than 2 then 5 then 5) and confirm the result is identical.

Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.63 ("In two rows of repeating coloured stars, determine when the blue stars will next meet.") — students identify the repeat lengths from the pattern and compute their LCM using the combined procedure, articulating why the LCM gives the meeting position.

Figure it Out Q2, section 11.3 p.63 ("(a) Is 5×7×11×11 a multiple of 5×7×7×11×2? (b) Is 5×7×11×11 a factor of....") — students decide each question by comparing prime factorisations directly, without computing the numbers, practising the subpart view. Figure it Out Q3, section 11.3 p.63 ("Find the HCF and LCM (stating answers as prime factorisations) of....") follows, with students expressing answers in factorised form.

Students reflect: which procedure — prime factorisation listing or the combined division — is more efficient for large numbers? They write one sentence justifying their preference and share with a neighbour.

periods.teacher_notes: The combined division procedure is new notation for students who have only seen factor trees; make sure they understand that the divisors in the left column form the HCF and that the LCM is assembled from those divisors and the final row of quotients. A common error is forgetting to include the final quotients in the LCM — a worked example on the board with coloured chalk for each component helps.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: HCF and LCM in Context: Folklore, Cubes, and Divisibility

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 11.3 p.63
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find two numbers whose HCF is 1 and LCM is 66.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 11.3 p.63
textbook_items_in_class.description: Karnataka folklore problem: a cowherd's cows pass in equal groups through crossings of 3, 5, and 7 gates; with fewer than 200 cows, find how many cows he had.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: A box is 12 cm × 18 cm × 36 cm; decide which cubes of side (a) 9 cm; (b) 6 cm; (c) 4 cm; (d) 3 cm; (e) 2 cm can be packed without gaps.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 11.3 p.64
homework.description: Choose the largest number that perfectly divides both 306 and 36 from (a) 36; (b) 612; (c) 18; (d) 3; (e) 2; (f) 360.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q4, section 11.3 p.63 ("Find two numbers whose HCF is 1 and LCM is 66.") — students factorise 66 = 2×3×11 and reason that if two numbers are co-prime (HCF = 1) their LCM equals their product, so the numbers must be a partition of the prime factors. Several valid pairs are possible; the class collects them all.

Figure it Out Q5, section 11.3 p.63 ("Karnataka folklore problem: a cowherd's cows pass in equal groups through crossings of 3, 5, and 7 gates....") — students translate the conditions into a divisibility requirement (the count must be divisible by 3, 5, and 7 simultaneously), compute LCM(3, 5, 7) = 105, and verify 105 < 200 while the next multiple 210 > 200.

Figure it Out Q6, section 11.3 p.64 ("A box is 12 cm × 18 cm × 36 cm; decide which cubes of side (a) 9 cm....") — students recognise that a cube fits without gaps when its side is a common factor of all three dimensions. They find the common factors of 12, 18, 36 and check each given side length against this list.

Students present the cube-packing reasoning to the class and generalise: a cube of side k packs the box exactly when k is a common factor of all three dimensions, and the largest such cube corresponds to the HCF of the three dimensions. Teacher confirms the HCF of 12, 18, 36 = 6 cm.

periods.teacher_notes: In the cowherd problem, students sometimes list multiples of 3, 5, and 7 separately and search for a common entry rather than computing the LCM — both are valid but the LCM route is far more efficient for larger constraints; make this comparison explicit. The cube-packing problem beautifully extends HCF to three numbers and can serve as a bridge to the homework item on choosing the largest common divisor.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: Puzzles, Games, and Mahaviracharya: LCM in Rich Contexts

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the smallest number divisible by 3, 4, 5, and 7 that leaves a remainder of 10 when divided by 11.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: In 'Fire in the Mountain', no one is out for 6 or 9 but some are out for 10; choose how many children could have been playing initially from (a) 72; (b) 90; (c) 45; (d) 3; (e) 36; (f) None of these.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: Tick the correct statement(s) about the LCM of two different primes (m, n): (a) less than both; (b) between the two; (c) greater than both; (d) less than m×n; (e) greater than m×n.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q9, section 11.3 p.64 ("In 'Fire in the Mountain', no one is out for 6 or 9 but some are out for 10....") — students play a quick classroom version of the elimination game with counts of 6, 9, and 10, identify which group sizes lead to the stated outcome, and then work the multiple-choice reasoning: the total must not be a multiple of 6 or 9 but must be a multiple of 10.

Figure it Out Q10, section 11.3 p.64 ("Tick the correct statement(s) about the LCM of two different primes (m, n)....") — students evaluate each statement independently, using the definition of prime (factors only 1 and itself) and the maximum-exponent rule to determine the LCM of two distinct primes is their product m×n. They tick correct options and write one sentence justifying the rejection of each incorrect option.

Figure it Out Q8, section 11.3 p.64 ("Find the smallest number divisible by 3, 4, 5, and 7 that leaves a remainder of 10 when divided by 11.") — students compute LCM(3, 4, 5, 7) = 420 first, then systematically check multiples of 420 for the remainder condition. Teacher guides the search strategy: list 420, 840, 1260,... and test each mod 11.

Brief preview of Mahaviracharya's fraction-sum problem in Figure it Out Q13, section 11.3 p.64 ("Find the smallest number that is a multiple of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10.") — students identify this as an LCM-of-denominators problem and write the setup.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'Fire in the Mountain' problem requires students to reason about what the total must and must not be a multiple of — a good moment to revisit the distinction between HCF and LCM conditions. For Figure it Out Q10, some students will tick option (d) incorrectly; ask them to test m = 2, n = 3 to find LCM = 6 = m×n, showing equality not inequality.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: Dog, Rabbit, and Mahaviracharya: Final Contextual Applications

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: A dog chasing a rabbit with a 150 ft head start jumps 9 ft each time the rabbit jumps 7 ft; find in how many leaps the dog catches up.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the smallest number that is a multiple of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q13, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mahaviracharya's problem (850 CE): add 8/15, 1/20, 7/36, 11/63, and 1/21, and find an efficient way to compute the sum (using the LCM of the denominators).

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q11, section 11.3 p.64 ("A dog chasing a rabbit with a 150 ft head start jumps 9 ft each time the rabbit jumps 7 ft....") — students set up the chase as a difference problem: the dog gains 2 ft per leap pair. With a 150 ft head start they divide 150 ÷ 2 = 75 leaps. Teacher draws out the connection to LCM thinking by asking at which leap-counts both land on the same position.

Figure it Out Q12, section 11.3 p.64 ("Find the smallest number that is a multiple of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10.") — students compute LCM(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10) using the combined division procedure, building the factorisation step by step.

Figure it Out Q13, section 11.3 p.64 ("Mahaviracharya's problem (850 CE): add 8/15, 1/20, 7/36, 11/63, and 1/21....") — students find the LCM of the five denominators (15, 20, 36, 63, 21), convert each fraction, and compute the sum. Teacher notes that Mahaviracharya described this procedure in the Ganitasarasangraha and invites students to reflect on the role of LCM in simplifying fraction arithmetic.

Students write one sentence each summarising the key strategy used in today's problems — either a difference approach, a multi-number LCM, or a common-denominator approach — and share with a neighbour to check for accuracy.

periods.teacher_notes: The dog-and-rabbit problem is sometimes misread as an LCM problem when it is a difference-of-rates problem; clarify the two distinct structures so students do not over-apply LCM. The Mahaviracharya context is a genuine historical connection — noting that the method in their textbook was described over 1100 years ago can spark curiosity about the history of mathematics.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: Common Ground: Four Problems, Three Methods
periods.teacher_notes: Refer to Prepared Table (see material: 'Problems and solutions') for the problems in full and their worked solutions. Pose all four problems on the board at once. Students work individually with full written working — no pair talk yet. Then groups of three compare answers; any disagreement is reconstructed step by step on paper before the group agrees. Four volunteers present one problem each; after each presentation the class names aloud the chapter method used. Problem 1 needs HCF by prime factorisation (take each common prime the minimum number of times). Problem 2 needs LCM by prime factorisation (take each prime the maximum number of times). Problem 3 needs the HCF × LCM = product property. Problem 4 needs generalisation — recognising when one number is a factor of the other and stating the HCF and LCM directly. Watch for students who multiply all primes for the HCF (confusing it with LCM), and for those who forget to check the divisibility constraint in Problem 4 before making their general claim.

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | A gardener has two lengths of rope: 126 cm and 210 cm. She wants to cut both into pieces of equal length, with no rope left over, using the longest possible pieces. How long should each piece be? | Prime factorise: 126 = 2×3×3×7 and 210 = 2×3×5×7. Common primes, minimum times each: one 2, one 3, one 7. HCF = 2×3×7 = 42. Each piece is 42 cm long.
2 | Two warning lights at a level crossing flash together at the start. One flashes every 18 seconds and the other every 24 seconds. After how many seconds will they next flash together? | Prime factorise: 18 = 2×3×3 and 24 = 2×2×2×3. Take each prime the maximum number of times: three 2s, two 3s. LCM = 8×9 = 72. They next flash together after 72 seconds.
3 | The HCF of two numbers is 12 and their LCM is 180. One of the numbers is 36. Find the other number. | HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers. So 12×180 = 36 × other. Other = 2160 ÷ 36 = 60. The other number is 60. Check: 36 = 2×2×3×3 and 60 = 2×2×3×5; HCF = 2×2×3 = 12 ✓; LCM = 2×2×3×3×5 = 180 ✓.
4 | Riya says: 'Whenever I pick any number n and the number 7n, their HCF is always n and their LCM is always 7n.' Is she right? Write a general statement and explain why. | Yes. Since 7n = 7×n, the number n is a factor of 7n. When one number is a factor of the other, the HCF is the smaller number and the LCM is the larger. So HCF(n, 7n) = n and LCM(n, 7n) = 7n for any positive whole number n. This works because n divides 7n exactly, so every common factor of n and 7n is also a factor of n, making n itself the greatest.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes all four problems on the board and reads each aloud. Students copy the problems into their exercise books. No discussion yet — the class moves straight to individual work.

Students work all four problems individually, writing every step. The room is quiet. Teacher circulates, noting which problems surface errors, but gives no answers — only asks 'What does the prime factorisation of that number look like?' if a student is stuck at the start.

Groups of three form and compare working. Where answers disagree, the group reconstructs both solutions line by line to locate the divergence and agree on the correct step. Each group also prepares to name, for each problem, the chapter method it used.

Four volunteers present one problem each at the board — full working, not just the answer. After each presentation the class calls out the chapter method: 'HCF by prime factorisation', 'LCM by prime factorisation', 'HCF times LCM equals product', or 'generalisation — factor-of property'. The teacher corrects any remaining errors on the spot.

Teacher closes with one sentence spoken to the class and written on the board: 'Every problem today yielded because prime factorisation shows exactly what two numbers share and what they do not — that common ground is what the whole chapter is about.' No further task is set.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly states what the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of two numbers is?

options.label: A
options.text: The greatest number that is a factor of both numbers.

options.label: B
options.text: The product of all prime factors of both numbers.

options.label: C
options.text: The smallest number that is a multiple of both numbers.

options.label: D
options.text: The sum of all common factors of both numbers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The HCF is the greatest number that is a factor of both numbers — option B.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition of HCF as the greatest among all common factors of two numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused HCF with LCM, recalling 'smallest common' instead of 'greatest common'.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is mixing up the prime-factorisation procedure (listing all prime factors) with the definition of HCF.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the identity of the HCF with a computed sum of common factors, a non-standard operation.

inclusivity.support: Look back at the tiling story in section 11.1 — the largest tile side that fits both 12 ft and 16 ft exactly is the HCF.
inclusivity.challenge: Write your own definition of HCF using the word 'subpart' of a prime factorisation, and check it matches the one above.

exercise.description: 'Jump Jackpot' game: for treasures on (a) 14 and 30; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 30 and 50; (d) 28 and 42, find the longest jump size from 0 that lands on both numbers, and explain why it equals their HCF.

items.prompt: The prime factorisation of 90 is 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. How many factors does 90 have in total (including 1 and 90 itself)?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count factors by adding 1 to each prime's exponent in the factorisation and multiplying the results.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student only counted the distinct prime factors (2, 3, 5) and their product 90 — a severe undercount.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student likely listed only the obvious small factors (1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 10 or similar) without a systematic approach.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have added exponents (1 + 2 + 1) and then multiplied incorrectly, or confused factor count with prime factor count.

inclusivity.support: Write 90 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 and list factor pairs systematically: 1×90, 2×45, 3×30, 5×18, 6×15, 9×10.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a number with exactly 6 factors, express it using prime factorisation, and explain why exactly 6 factors result.

exercise.description: List all the factors of (a) 90; (b) 105; (c) 132; (d) 360 (24 factors); (e) 840 (32 factors), using prime factorisation.

items.prompt: Two friends count aloud in a circle. One calls out every 4th number as 'idli' and the other calls every 6th number as 'vada'. What is the first number at which both call out together?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The first common call-out is the LCM of 4 and 6. Since 4 = 2² and 6 = 2×3, LCM = 2²×3 = 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the LCM of 4 and 6 by taking the maximum exponent of each prime: 2²×3 = 12.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added 4 and 6, using addition instead of identifying the smallest common multiple.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student computed the product 4×6 = 24, confusing the product of the numbers with their LCM.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student found the HCF (the largest number that divides both) rather than the LCM.

inclusivity.support: List the first several multiples of 4 and the first several multiples of 6, and circle the first number that appears in both lists.
inclusivity.challenge: Explain in one sentence why the first common call-out is always the LCM and never just any common multiple.

exercise.description: 'Idli-Vada' game: for the number pairs (a) 4 and 6; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 14 and 30; (d) 15 and 55, find the first number for which 'idli-vada' is called out, and decide whether the answer is always the LCM.

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: Riya says: 'The HCF of any two consecutive whole numbers is always 1.' Test this claim with three different pairs of consecutive whole numbers, state whether you agree or disagree with Riya, and give a brief reason based on the prime factorisations of the two numbers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Testing pairs such as (5, 6), (10, 11), (15, 16) shows the HCF is 1 in each case. The general reason: consecutive whole numbers n and n+1 cannot share any prime factor p, because p would then divide their difference (n+1) − n = 1, which is impossible for any prime p > 1. So their only common factor is 1, and HCF = 1. Riya is correct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reason that a prime dividing both n and n+1 would divide their difference 1, which no prime can do, so HCF = 1 always.

inclusivity.support: Talk through your reasoning with a partner before writing — say aloud why 7 cannot divide both 14 and 15.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the claim: what if the two numbers differ by 2 instead of 1? Adjust the argument and state when the HCF can be greater than 1.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.59
exercise.description: Make and explain a general statement about the HCF of (a) two consecutive even numbers; (b) two consecutive odd numbers; (c) two even numbers; (d) two consecutive numbers; (e) two co-prime numbers.

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: Arjun says: 'The LCM of two co-prime numbers is always equal to their product.' Write a general statement using algebra to describe two co-prime numbers and use the prime-factorisation rule for LCM to justify why Arjun's claim is true.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two co-prime numbers m and n share no common prime factor, so their prime factorisations are completely disjoint. By the LCM rule — take each prime the maximum number of times it appears in either factorisation — the LCM contains every prime from m's factorisation and every prime from n's factorisation. This gives LCM = m × n. Arjun is correct; the algebraic description is: for any two whole numbers m and n with HCF(m, n) = 1, LCM(m, n) = m × n.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the maximum-exponent LCM rule: disjoint prime sets means all primes are selected from both, giving LCM = product.

inclusivity.support: First try m = 4 and n = 9 — write both prime factorisations, list the LCM, then compare it to 4 × 9.
inclusivity.challenge: Does HCF × LCM = product still hold for co-prime pairs? Substitute HCF = 1 and verify the identity algebraically.

items.prompt: Meena has two pieces of ribbon, one 48 cm long and the other 60 cm long. She wants to cut both ribbons into pieces of the same length, with no ribbon left over, and she wants each piece to be as long as possible. What is the longest possible length of each piece? Show your working using prime factorisation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁴ × 3 and 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 2² × 3 × 5. Common primes: take minimum exponents — two 2s and one 3. HCF = 2² × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12. The longest possible piece length is 12 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find HCF(48, 60) by taking each common prime the minimum number of times: 2² × 3 = 12.

inclusivity.support: Draw factor trees for 48 and 60, circle primes that appear in both trees, and pick the smallest exponent for each.
inclusivity.challenge: If Meena adds a third piece of ribbon that is 84 cm long, find the longest common piece length for all three ribbons.

exercise.description: Find the common factors and HCF of (a) 50, 60; (b) 140, 275; (c) 77, 725; (d) 370, 592; (e) 81, 243.

items.prompt: A school bell rings every 8 minutes and a factory siren sounds every 18 minutes. Both ring together at 9:00 am. After how many minutes will they next ring together? Show your working using prime factorisation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3 = 2 × 3². Taking the maximum exponent of each prime: three 2s and two 3s. LCM = 2³ × 3² = 8 × 9 = 72. They will next ring together after 72 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find LCM(8, 18) by taking each prime the maximum number of times it appears in either factorisation: 2³ × 3² = 72.

inclusivity.support: List the first several multiples of 8 (8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 64, 72, ...) and of 18 (18, 36, 54, 72, ...) and find the first one in common.
inclusivity.challenge: A third alarm rings every 12 minutes. Find the next time all three ring together, using the prime-factorisation LCM method for three numbers.

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: In a pattern strip, red stars repeat every 6 positions and blue stars repeat every 10 positions. Both colours appear at position 1. At which position do a red star and a blue star next appear together? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 = 2 × 3 and 10 = 2 × 5. LCM = 2 × 3 × 5 = 30. The red and blue stars next coincide at position 31 (that is, 30 positions after position 1). If the question asks for the number of positions ahead: 30.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find LCM(6, 10) = 2 × 3 × 5 = 30; the two stars next meet 30 positions after their first common position.

inclusivity.support: Write out the positions of red stars (1, 7, 13, 19, 25, 31, ...) and blue stars (1, 11, 21, 31, ...) and find the first position after 1 that appears in both lists.
inclusivity.challenge: Add a third colour that repeats every 15 positions. Find the first position beyond 1 where all three colours appear together.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.63
exercise.description: In two rows of repeating coloured stars, determine when the blue stars will next meet.

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: Two numbers have an HCF of 1 and a product of 77. Find all possible pairs of numbers that satisfy these conditions. Show how you use the prime factorisation of 77 to determine the pairs.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 77 = 7 × 11. Since HCF = 1, the two numbers must be co-prime (share no common prime factor). The factor pairs of 77 are (1, 77) and (7, 11). HCF(1, 77) = 1 ✓ and HCF(7, 11) = 1 ✓. Both pairs satisfy the conditions. So the possible pairs are (1, 77) and (7, 11).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Factorise 77 = 7 × 11, list all factor pairs, and keep those with HCF = 1 (co-prime pairs).

inclusivity.support: List all ways to write 77 as a product of two whole numbers, then check which pairs share no common factor other than 1.
inclusivity.challenge: Replace 77 with 66 and find all co-prime factor pairs of 66 — notice there are more possibilities when the number has more distinct prime factors.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 11.3 p.63
exercise.description: Find two numbers whose HCF is 1 and LCM is 66.

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: Find the smallest whole number greater than 1 that is divisible by 4, 6, and 9. Show your working using prime factorisation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 = 2², 6 = 2 × 3, 9 = 3². Taking the maximum exponent of each prime: two 2s and two 3s. LCM = 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36. The smallest such number is 36. Verification: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 ✓, 36 ÷ 6 = 6 ✓, 36 ÷ 9 = 4 ✓.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute LCM(4, 6, 9) by taking maximum prime exponents: 2² × 3² = 36.

inclusivity.support: Write the prime factorisation of each of the three numbers in a table and underline the largest power of each prime across the three rows before multiplying.
inclusivity.challenge: Is there a number smaller than 36 that is divisible by any two of these three numbers? Which pairs share a smaller common multiple, and why?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 11.3 p.64
exercise.description: Find the smallest number divisible by 3, 4, 5, and 7 that leaves a remainder of 10 when divided by 11.

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: A cat jumps 5 ft at a time and a squirrel jumps 3 ft at a time, both starting from the same spot. After how many jumps will the cat first land on a position the squirrel has also landed on? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The cat's landing positions are multiples of 5 and the squirrel's are multiples of 3. The first common position is LCM(5, 3). Since 5 and 3 are co-prime (no shared prime factor), LCM = 5 × 3 = 15. The cat reaches position 15 after 15 ÷ 5 = 3 jumps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find LCM(5, 3) = 15 (co-prime product), then divide by the cat's jump length to count its jumps: 15 ÷ 5 = 3.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line and mark the cat's positions (5, 10, 15, 20, ...) and the squirrel's positions (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, ...) to find the first common landing.
inclusivity.challenge: A third animal jumps 7 ft at a time. Find the first position where all three land together, and how many jumps each animal makes to reach it.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 11.3 p.64
exercise.description: A dog chasing a rabbit with a 150 ft head start jumps 9 ft each time the rabbit jumps 7 ft; find in how many leaps the dog catches up.

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: The HCF of two numbers is 12 and their LCM is 180. One of the numbers is 36. Find the other number. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Using the property HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers: 12 × 180 = 2160. If one number is 36, the other = 2160 ÷ 36 = 60. Verification: HCF(36, 60) — 36 = 2²×3² and 60 = 2²×3×5, so HCF = 2²×3 = 12 ✓ and LCM = 2²×3²×5 = 180 ✓.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers: other number = (12 × 180) ÷ 36 = 60.

inclusivity.support: Write out the formula HCF × LCM = first number × second number, substitute the known values, and solve for the unknown.
inclusivity.challenge: Verify your answer by writing the prime factorisation of both numbers and checking that the HCF and LCM match what was given.
